hints: Look first at where the CH2OH group is in each diagram, it should be on the carbon at the top left of the ring, pointing up.
Now check the OH on carbon 1 on the right side of the ring, for alpha-glucose it must point down below the ring, not up.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes glucose, glucose**

Glucose in its ring form is a six-membered ring with five carbons and one oxygen. The CH2OH group is always attached to carbon 5, shown at the top left of these diagrams, and it points up.

This immediately rules out any diagram with CH2OH at the bottom.

**Recall what makes alpha, alpha**

Alpha and beta glucose differ only at carbon 1, the carbon on the right side of the ring. In alpha-glucose, the OH on carbon 1 points down, below the plane of the ring. In beta-glucose, it points up.

So we are looking for CH2OH up at the top, plus OH down on the right.

**Match to the diagrams**

Only diagram A has both features: CH2OH up on the top left carbon, and OH down on the carbon 1 on the right. It also shows the correct glucose pattern of OH groups on the other carbons. That is alpha-glucose.

options.A: Correct. CH2OH is up at the top and the OH on carbon 1 is down on the right, which is the definition of alpha-glucose.
options.B: Incorrect. The CH2OH group is at the bottom of the ring instead of the top, so this cannot be glucose in the standard orientation.
options.C: Incorrect. CH2OH is at the bottom and the OH on carbon 1 points up, which would be beta, not alpha.
options.D: Incorrect. Although CH2OH is correctly up, the OH on carbon 1 points up, so this is beta-glucose, not alpha-glucose.
